source_first_reader_routes: Leopold II: acceptance of French constitution
referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Monarchs had different priorities; Gustavus actively wanted intervention, Catherine sought freedom of action in Poland, and Leopold treated Louis’s constitutional acceptance as removing the need to act. A unified anti-French crusade is misleading here.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The owned Catherine and Gustavus treatments cover differing aims; lead must adjudicate Pillnitz’s conditionality and Leopold’s response as a whole record.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Civil conflict and inconsistent metropolitan policies helped form the context for the slave uprising. Communication delays made responses obsolete; antislavery commitments and port dependence on slavery created distinct political embarrassments.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The colonial crisis belongs to the lead-owned slave-revolt record; commodity effects are represented by the owned shortages subject. No whole-record approval of the colonial subject is claimed.

source_first_reader_routes: Dumouriez: treason and failed march on Paris
referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Defeat and soldiers’ refusal to march on Paris led Dumouriez to defect. French withdrawal of open-ended international aid and peace overtures were read as weakness rather than moderation.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Owned military-crisis/fraternity subjects preserve defeat and conciliatory response; Dumouriez’s whole trajectory and inconsistent defection dates require lead disposition.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Early recovery preceded the full effect of mass mobilization. February conscription met resistance; August requisition mobilized military-age single men plus labor, transport, buildings and materials throughout society.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The owned early-victory record and lead-owned February/August mobilization records distinguish early recovery from subsequent mass recruitment.

source_first_reader_routes: Glorious First of June: convoy objective
referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Fleurus was the decisive turning point. Naval battle losses must be distinguished from success in protecting the grain convoy; technical and organizational contributions merit access alongside named victories.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Fleurus and naval strategic success have distinct owned retrieval; Toulon and Bonaparte’s recapture role remain lead-owned.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Renewed Belgian annexation sustained Austrian and British resistance. British Caribbean ambitions combined planter protection, suppression of slave rebellion and commerce; costly expeditions did not subdue Guadeloupe or Saint-Domingue.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Chapter9 supports strategic/colonial limits, not a developed human-cost claim. Direct reinspection of413 supports the separate proposed British Saint-Domingue mortality/withdrawal extension; lead must re-review the enlarged cross-chapter record.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Tone’s nonsectarian reform network and exile advocacy promoted intervention. Hoche’s rivalry and French desire to reciprocate subversion aided plans; weather defeated the expedition, and Doyle doubts that landing at that place and time would have produced the promised rising.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The lead-owned Irish record is the proper locus for differing readiness/geography and the source’s doubts about a successful landing; no partial approval is implied.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Purge of moderates hardened negotiations. Campo Formio recognized French gains and sister republics but could not bind the Empire over the Rhine; British willingness to concede European conquests still fell short of French demands for colonial restitution.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The owned Bonaparte-authority record supplies his political role; the settlements and negotiation limits are lead-owned distinct requirements.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Better republican garrisons suppressed open Breton revolt and enforced quotas, while resistance continued as guerrilla warfare. This differs from the initial territorial success of the Vendée armies.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Refer to lead for prose226 Breton guerrilla distinction;225 map labels cannot supply the substantive requirement.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Opposition to local Jacobin extremism spread among people who had accepted republic and regicide; local club rivalries and sectional organization distinguish these cases from straightforward royalism.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The Marseilles case is owned. Nîmes, Aix, Arles and Avignon qualifications belong to the lead-owned Federalist whole subject and should be preserved through its local-variation treatment rather than inferred from the map.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Cities coordinated resistance unevenly; several frontier centers drew back from rebellion. Lyons’s execution of Chalier deepened the conflict beyond constitutional protest.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Local cooperation and hesitation in Montpellier/Toulouse/Grenoble are prose qualifications on239; retain them under the lead’s Federalist variation requirement, not a universal revolt claim.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Regional solidarity with purged deputies and constitutional protest coexisted uneasily with royalist military and social support. Girondin republicanism disappointed some hosts; Wimpffen’s possible English pay remains uncertain.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Caen/Normandy/Brittany is owned. Jura and Wimpffen’s uncertain English connection require the lead’s Federalist context; uncertainty must remain uncertainty.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Doyle rejects inflated claims that most departments revolted and the idea of deliberate republican breakup. Leaders chiefly wanted a tranquil propertied republic; conscription, forced loans, policing and price controls provoked broader support than wealth alone explains.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Extent and constitutional meaning must use241–242 prose. The caption-only map cannot answer extent/significance; lead has undertaken that task correction.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: The constitution deliberately won popular assent through direct annual elections, expanded rights and legislative control of executive power. Ratification and ceremonial promulgation did not produce implementation; wartime emergency justified indefinite suspension.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Direct elections, social rights and ratification/nonimplementation are represented in the lead-owned Constitution whole subject; review lead retains responsibility for completeness.

source_first_reader_routes: Committee of Public Safety: authority and limits
referrals.source_first_analytical_note: The Committee mobilized leadership without initially becoming an undisputed government. War reverses, internal revolt and contested Parisian power formed the setting for its expansion.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: The owned Terror-emergence record covers crisis; committee authority, Carnot/Prieur and disputed Hanriot control are referred to lead’s government/mobilization review.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: The ascendant radicals first silenced their radical rivals. Democratic constitutional implementation was explicitly deferred, and temporary emergency government justified central direction.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Lead must keep suppression of enragés, suspension of the constitution and emergency government as separate linked treatments; related labels alone do not establish coverage.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Loss of commanding heights forced allied evacuation; refugees escaped, but mass shootings and commission trials followed. Strategic naval value limited further destruction despite the scale of perceived betrayal.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Toulon’s recapture, Port-de-la-Montagne and limits to demolition are lead-owned; no approval of that whole record from my page inspection.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: The law established reporting chains and prohibited local reinterpretation, bypassed departments for emergency functions, and suppressed unofficial bodies. Implementation was gradual and resisted; constitutional decentralization remained an ideal deferred to peace.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Owned provincial autonomy/recall is one part; full institutional chains, departments and national agents belong to the lead-owned government record.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Local 1790 price bases created uneven incentives; transport and profit adjustments followed. Wage limits were scarcely enforced initially, black markets persisted and military buying competed with controls; central schedules nevertheless expanded practical regulation.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Refer to lead for price bases, transport/profit adjustments, wage enforcement, black markets and military competition; these are distinct mechanisms within Maximum, not a label-only match.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Real corruption and a real royalist intriguer were woven into a much broader alleged foreign plot. Discovery of Fabre’s corruption broke Robespierre’s confidence in the Indulgents; preserve the difference between evidence and inferred conspiracy.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Owned scandal and Hébertist accusation records distinguish real fraud from invented conspiracy. Ask lead to retain the reality of deBatz as an intriguer without validating the encompassing foreign plot.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Robespierre tied democratic government to civic virtue and subordinated private interest to public good, while rejecting continuous direct action by the sovereign people. These arguments informed suspicion of moral deviation.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Refer to lead’s Robespierre whole-record review: civic virtue, private/public interest and rejection of continuous direct popular intervention are substantive claims.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: The committees’ motives and internal deliberations are poorly evidenced. Danton was tried on broad political allegations rather than corruption; a misleading report excluded defendants when their insistence on witnesses threatened conviction. Doyle interprets punishment as increasingly preventive and moralized, but explicitly retains uncertainty about motives.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Lead owns the trial and motives; owned preventive-Terror interpretation retains uncertainty and must not recast allegations as proven corruption.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: State control of the Commune brought wage repression and destruction of remaining protest institutions. July wage tables imposed cuts after earlier nominal increases, helping alienate workers.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Institutional destruction is owned; wage cuts and the LeChapelier constraint belong to lead Maximum review and explain later popular nonmobilization.

source_first_reader_routes: Robespierre: assessment of power and intentions
referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Doyle explicitly denies that Robespierre was a dictator or that reliable evidence proves he aimed to become one. Moral inflexibility and threats helped destroy him; survivors used the accusation to shift responsibility for acts they had shared.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Refer to lead: the explicit denial that Robespierre was a dictator or demonstrably aimed to be one is stronger than a vague warning against omnipotence; preserve it in parent stance.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Devastation and conscription prolonged insurgency. Religious concessions, amnesty, exemption and retained arms purchased apparent peace, but leaders’ motives differed and British expedition plans made some truces tactical.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Lead-owned western-peace and insurgency records must retain tactical truces, retained arms and competing British expectations rather than treating pacification as completed reconciliation.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Disarmament and detention marked former activists as targets. Counter-terror included royalists but was mostly retaliatory and locally anarchic; its scale and danger varied sharply by region.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Owned disarmament and enabling of vengeance connect to lead-owned WhiteTerror; preserve early incidents preceding the April law.

source_first_reader_routes: Prison massacres: Lyons, Aix, Tarascon, Marseilles
referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Royalist networks and revenge gangs overlapped. Southeastern massacres often benefited from official connivance; Toulon’s pro-Jacobin response shows that anti-Jacobin reaction was not uniform.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Correct both owned Toulon evidence locators from293 to292. Lead owns wider WhiteTerror group names and southeast geography.

referrals.source_first_analytical_note: Economic distress encouraged monarchist sentiment, but Provence’s declaration promised extensive restoration and excluded regicides from amnesty while leaving national lands unresolved. It undermined negotiated restoration and constitutional monarchism.
referrals.reconciliation_reason: Refer to lead for the Constitution revision and LouisXVIII whole records: Verona’s restoration conditions and alienation of property holders qualify monarchist hopes.
